You are the writer of the discussion described below. You write out the discussion that the participants listed below take part in, under the rules and the flow given.

## Setting
Setting the cleaning arrangement for the shared areas. Five housemates share a kitchen, a bathroom, and a living room, and the informal habit they started with has stopped working. They are settling on one arrangement for the coming year. Participants: Rin, Ryuji, Daisuke, Mio and Victoria. Each participant has a concern of their own, which the others do not know.
Things that can be looked into (titles only):
- Bathroom spray stock and the tin's receipts
- Management office rate sheet and billing
- Stopwatch timing of a full pass
- Standard terms of the outside firm
- Bathroom grout after the July scrub
- What each housemate counts as done
- Absences on the wall calendar
- A fortnight's watch on kitchen use
- Rows recorded in the house chat
- Note left by the previous tenants

## Discussion format
The talk proceeds in rounds. Each round has 4 turns; in each turn, every participant speaks once, in this fixed order: Ryuji, Mio, Victoria, Rin and Daisuke. On a turn, a participant either speaks, says "Skip" (passes this turn only), or says "Over" (takes no further turns this round). A participant can address another directly with @Name, to ask them a question, answer theirs, agree with them, or object to what they said. An utterance is anywhere from 1 to 40 words; give it the length and content that suit the moment. An utterance consists only of the participant's own words: no name labels, headings, stage directions or commentary, and no speaking for others. The talk is a conversation among the participants: they respond to one another, asking, answering, agreeing and objecting, and the decision grows out of that exchange.

## Schedule
| Round | Start of the round | Talk | End of the round |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | nothing new (the things that can be looked into are listed above, titles only) | 4 turns | each participant chooses 2 of the listed things to look into |
| 2 | each participant is told what they found out (that participant only) | 4 turns | nothing |
| 3 | everyone is told the options | 4 turns | every participant votes; the option with the most votes is adopted |
- Several participants may choose the same thing; what is found out is told only to the participant who looked into it.
If votes are tied, one of the tied options is chosen by a fixed rule. The discussion ends after the vote.

## Looking into things
After round 1, each participant chooses 2 of the listed things to look into. What they find out is told only to that participant.

## Participants

## Hidden information
The options and the full text of every card are listed here. The participants do not know them before the schedule above says so, and nothing from them may appear in the talk before the round in which it is revealed.

Options (see the schedule above):
- A: Standing Assignments. Each person takes permanent ownership of particular areas for as long as they live there, choosing their own timing rather than following a shared calendar.
- B: Fixed Weekly Rota. Each area is assigned to one person for a named week, rotating through the household in a published order that repeats until someone asks for it to be revised.
- C: Paid Cleaning Service. An outside cleaner comes on a set schedule for the shared areas, with the household handling the arrangements and settling the invoice among themselves each month.

Cards (see the schedule above; title: text):
- Bathroom spray stock and the tin's receipts: There are three part-used bottles of the same bathroom spray in the cupboard, and the tin's receipts come to about 2,300 yen a month, much of it bought twice.
- Management office rate sheet and billing: The management office's rate sheet posts a contracted cleaner at 4,200 yen an hour, and the bill goes to one named tenant who then collects from everyone else.
- Stopwatch timing of a full pass: A housemate ran a stopwatch on a proper pass last Sunday: the hob and kitchen floor came to forty-seven minutes, the bathroom thirty-five, the living room twenty.
- Standard terms of the outside firm: The cleaning firm's standard terms give a two-hour arrival window and say anything left on a surface is worked around, so someone must be in and tidy beforehand.
- Bathroom grout after the July scrub: A housemate marked the bathroom grout after scrubbing it in July and the black spotting was back inside eleven days; that small window is the only ventilation the bathroom has.
- What each housemate counts as done: Some of the housemates count a room done once the basin is wiped, others only after the floor and the drain, so its state swings with whoever last had it.
- Absences on the wall calendar: The wall calendar shows two of the five away for a week or more in most months, and one housemate was gone for the whole of August.
- A fortnight's watch on kitchen use: A fortnight of watching the kitchen found that nearly everything that piles up in there comes from two or three housemates cooking, while the rest only make coffee.
- Rows recorded in the house chat: Scrolling back through the house chat, both of the rows the household has had started with one person reminding another about something that had not been done.
- Note left by the previous tenants: The previous tenants left a note inside the cupboard door saying they divided the rooms permanently, and that by the second year two of them barely spoke.

Write the complete transcript of the discussion in the exact Markdown format specified. Output only the transcript.

Markdown, exactly this structure; nothing before or after it:
